summary:
This Devon Ice Cap project turns six NASA-ISRO NISAR radar images into an interactive record of glacier motion on the Devon Island, located in Nunavut, Canada. You can play the September 5 to November 4, 2026 timelapse and compare how far two glaciers moved inland and near their shared ocean front. Note that the glaciers move at a glacial pace.

The Southeast 1 glacier moved 12.4 metres eastward inland from September 17 to 29. Its inland displacement ranges from 9.8 to 12.4 metres per 12 days over the four intervals ending November 4. We checked the measurements against apparent motion on the stationary bedrock and made sure to flag any estimates that were uncertain.

Whether Southeast 1 sped up at the ocean front remains an open question, but a sustained speed up there could actually deliver more land ice to the ocean and increase the amount of icebergs in the Hyde Inlet, where a surge that happened previously already brought in more icebergs.
details:
Has Southeast 1's inland speed up reached the ocean? Southeast 1 and Southeast 2 drain part of the Devon Ice Cap into Hyde Inlet through a shared glacier front. During a previous surge, some researchers documented more icebergs to the inlet and in 1979, a large calving event actually removed around 3 square kilometers from the southeast 1 side of that front in under two months! The Devon ice cap is the 4th largest ice cap in canada and the 7th largest in the world, so if faster flow happens to reach the coast and persists, then more inland ice could enter the ocean and contribute to sea level rise.

We used the L band HH channel from six NISAR level 2 GCOV acquisitions on the same descending track which gives us five 12 day comparisons consecutively. Radar lets us see the glacier through the clouds and without any sunlight required. We used Python, GDAL, NumPy and SciPy to match the radar texture in overlapping windows on a 10 metre grid. We made estimations to the shifts that are smaller than one pixel and checked matches in both directions. We also used the stationary bedrock to correct for any misalignment in the images. On held out bedrock, the 90th percentile of absolute eastward error ranged from 1.0 to 4.6 metres across the five pairs. We also varied the matching window size and made sure to flag if there were any estimates that changed materially.

Near the southeast 1's front, eastward displacement from 4.2 to 7.7 metres per 12 days in the final three intervals, and, in the first interval, southeast 1's estimated motion fell within bedrock scatter. The comparable earlier measurements would help date the inland speed up and test whether the coastal flow actually accelerated or not.

The HTML/CSS/JavaScript explorer lets visitors to the website play around with the radar timelapse and select either glacier to compare the inland and near front measurements. Its arrows are enlarged 42 times so metre scale motion is actually visible. The measurements and quality flags as well as source granule records are available inside this viewer as well. ChatGPT 6.1 was used to generate the website code.
